title: Der Arme und der Reiche
titleEn: The Poor Man and the Rich Man
part: The Poor Man and the Rich Man
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 87. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 87, from the days when the dear Lord still walked the earth himself. Benighted on the road, he is turned away by the rich man in the fine house and taken in by the poor couple across the way, who feed him potatoes and goat’s milk and give up their own bed for a heap of straw. In the morning he grants them three wishes — salvation, health and daily bread, and a new house — and the rich man, hearing of it, gallops after him and talks his way into three of his own. What follows is a small masterpiece of self-inflicted damage: an unruly horse, a saddle to carry home, and a wife who cannot get off it, all before he has thought of one thing he actually wants. Spelling follows the 1857 edition (daß, gieng, Thür, Rath, Muth, todt, roth).

sentences.t: Vor alten Zeiten, als der liebe Gott noch selber auf Erden unter den Menschen wandelte, trug es sich zu, daß er eines Abends müde war und ihn die Nacht überfiel, bevor er zu einer Herberge kommen konnte.
sentences.l: In old times, when the dear God still walked himself on earth among men, it came to pass that one evening he was tired and the night overtook him before he could come to an inn.
sentences.i: In olden times, when the dear Lord still walked the earth himself among men, it came to pass that one evening he was weary and night overtook him before he could reach an inn.
sentences.n: “trug es sich zu” — sich zutragen, to come to pass, happen; the prefix zu waits at the end of the clause. “eines Abends” is a genitive of time: one evening. der liebe Gott, the dear God, is the ordinary German name for God in these tales and is kept as such. Herberge is a shelter for the night, an inn taking travellers.

sentences.t: Nun standen auf dem Weg vor ihm zwei Häuser einander gegenüber, das eine groß und schön, das andere klein und ärmlich anzusehen, und gehörte das große einem Reichen, das kleine einem armen Manne.
sentences.l: Now there stood on the way before him two houses opposite one another, the one large and fine, the other small and poor to look at, and the large one belonged to a rich man, the small one to a poor man.
sentences.i: Now on the way before him two houses stood facing one another, the one large and fine, the other small and poor to look at; the large one belonged to a rich man, the small one to a poor man.
sentences.n: “anzusehen” is zu + infinitive after an adjective: poor to look at, poor in appearance. The second half drops its subject and begins with the verb — “und gehörte das große” — an old brevity English cannot copy. gehören takes the dative, so einem Reichen is “to a rich man.” Reicher and Armer are adjectives used as nouns, as the title of the tale has them.

sentences.t: Da dachte unser Herr Gott „dem Reichen werde ich nicht beschwerlich fallen: bei ihm will ich übernachten.“
sentences.l: Then our Lord God thought “to the rich man I shall not be burdensome: with him will I stay the night.”
sentences.i: Then our Lord God thought: “I shall not be a burden to the rich man; with him I will pass the night.”
sentences.n: “jemandem beschwerlich fallen” = to be a burden to someone, to put him out; the dative dem Reichen carries the person. übernachten is to spend the night. The thought is given as direct speech with no verb of saying beyond dachte — usual in these tales.

sentences.t: Der Reiche, als er an seine Thüre klopfen hörte, machte das Fenster auf und fragte den Fremdling was er suche?
sentences.l: The rich man, when he heard knocking at his door, opened the window and asked the stranger what he was seeking?
sentences.i: The rich man, hearing a knock at his door, opened the window and asked the stranger what he wanted.
sentences.n: suche is the subjunctive of reported speech — the tale reports the question rather than making it its own — and the question mark stands although nothing is quoted. “klopfen hörte” is hören + a bare infinitive, as English says “heard knocking.” Thüre is the 1857 spelling of Türe; machte … auf is separable aufmachen.

sentences.t: Der Herr antwortete „ich bitte um ein Nachtlager.“
sentences.l: The Lord answered “I ask for a night’s lodging.”
sentences.i: The Lord answered: “I ask for a bed for the night.”
sentences.n: “bitten um” = to ask for a thing. Nachtlager is a place to lie for the night, not necessarily a bed.

sentences.t: Der Reiche guckte den Wandersmann von Haupt bis zu den Füßen an, und weil der liebe Gott schlichte Kleider trug und nicht aussah wie einer, der viel Geld in der Tasche hat, schüttelte er mit dem Kopf und sprach „ich kann euch nicht aufnehmen, meine Kammern liegen voll Kräuter und Samen,
sentences.l: The rich man looked the wayfaring man over from head down to his feet, and because the dear God wore plain clothes and did not look like one who has much money in his pocket, he shook his head and spoke “I cannot take you in, my chambers lie full of herbs and seed,
sentences.i: The rich man eyed the wayfarer from head to foot; and because the dear Lord wore plain clothes and did not look like a man with much money in his pocket, he shook his head and said: “I cannot take you in — my rooms are full of herbs and seed,
sentences.n: guckte … an is angucken, the humbler cousin of ansehen, to look someone over — and its prefix an waits at the very end of a long clause, so hold it in mind until it arrives. “mit dem Kopf schütteln” = to shake one’s head. Haupt is the elevated word for head. The excuse is a householder’s: chambers packed with drying herbs and stored seed have no room for a guest.

sentences.t: und sollte ich einen jeden beherbergen, der an meine Thüre klopft, so könnte ich selber den Bettelstab in die Hand nehmen.
sentences.l: and should I lodge every one who knocks at my door, then I could take up the beggar’s staff myself.
sentences.i: and if I were to take in every man who knocks at my door, I might soon be going about with a beggar’s staff myself.
sentences.n: A conditional with no wenn: the verb comes first — “sollte ich einen jeden beherbergen” — and the answering clause opens with so, which English renders as “then.” “den Bettelstab in die Hand nehmen” is a fixed expression for being reduced to begging; the Bettelstab is the staff that marked a licensed beggar on the roads.

sentences.t: Sucht euch anderswo ein Auskommen.“
sentences.l: Seek yourselves a livelihood elsewhere.”
sentences.i: Look for a lodging somewhere else.”
sentences.n: Auskommen is what one gets by with — a living, and here what will see him through the night. sucht euch is the plural imperative with a reflexive dative: seek for yourself. The rich man says ihr to the stranger throughout, the ordinary polite plural of the tales.

sentences.t: Schlug damit sein Fenster zu und ließ den lieben Gott stehen.
sentences.l: Struck his window to with that and left the dear God standing.
sentences.i: With that he slammed his window shut and left the dear Lord standing there.
sentences.n: The sentence begins with its verb and no subject at all — “Schlug damit sein Fenster zu” — a curt narrative shorthand that matches the man’s rudeness. zuschlagen is separable: schlug … zu. “stehen lassen” = to leave someone standing, to walk out on him.

sentences.t: Also kehrte ihm der liebe Gott den Rücken und gieng hinüber zu dem kleinen Haus.
sentences.l: So the dear God turned his back on him and went over to the small house.
sentences.i: So the dear Lord turned his back on him and went across to the little house.
sentences.n: “jemandem den Rücken kehren” = to turn one’s back on someone, with the person in the dative: ihm. Also here means “thus, so,” not “also.” gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging.

sentences.t: Kaum hatte er angeklopft, so klinkte der Arme schon sein Thürchen auf und bat den Wandersmann einzutreten.
sentences.l: Hardly had he knocked, so the poor man already unlatched his little door and bade the wayfaring man step in.
sentences.i: Scarcely had he knocked when the poor man had already unlatched his little door and was bidding the wayfarer come in.
sentences.n: “Kaum hatte er … so …” — hardly had he, when; the verb stands first because kaum is fronted. Thürchen is the diminutive of Thür, and the diminutives here (Thürchen, later Fensterlein) quietly measure the smallness of the house. klinken is to work the latch; “bat … einzutreten” has zu + infinitive after bitten.

sentences.t: „Bleibt die Nacht über bei mir,“ sagte er „es ist schon finster, und heute könnt ihr doch nicht weiter kommen.“
sentences.l: “Stay the night through with me,” said he, “it is already dark, and today you cannot get any further after all.”
sentences.i: “Stay the night here with me,” he said; “it is dark already, and you will get no further today in any case.”
sentences.n: “die Nacht über” = through the night, over the night; über follows its noun. doch is the little word that concedes a fact both speakers can see — rendered here as “after all,” “in any case.” Bleibt and könnt are the plural forms: he too says ihr to the stranger.

sentences.t: Das gefiel dem lieben Gott und er trat zu ihm ein.
sentences.l: That pleased the dear God and he stepped in to him.
sentences.i: That pleased the dear Lord, and he went in with him.
sentences.n: gefallen takes the dative — literally “that was pleasing to the dear God.” eintreten is separable: trat … ein.

sentences.t: Die Frau des Armen reichte ihm die Hand, hieß ihn willkommen und sagte er möchte sichs bequem machen und vorlieb nehmen, sie hätten nicht viel, aber was es wäre, gäben sie von Herzen gerne.
sentences.l: The wife of the poor man reached him her hand, bade him welcome and said he might make himself comfortable and take what there was, they had not much, but what it was, they gave gladly from the heart.
sentences.i: The poor man’s wife gave him her hand, bade him welcome and said he should make himself comfortable and take pot-luck: they had not much, but such as it was they gave it with all their hearts.
sentences.n: From “er möchte” onwards everything is subjunctive of reported speech — möchte, hätten, wäre, gäben — so the tale gives her words without quoting them; English marks this only by the reporting frame. “vorlieb nehmen” is a fixed phrase: to be content with what is offered, to take pot-luck. sichs = sich es. “von Herzen gerne” = gladly, from the heart.

sentences.t: Dann setzte sie Kartoffeln ans Feuer, und derweil sie kochten, melkte sie ihre Ziege, damit sie ein wenig Milch dazu hätten.
sentences.l: Then she set potatoes to the fire, and while they were cooking she milked her goat, so that they might have a little milk to go with them.
sentences.i: Then she set potatoes on the fire, and while they cooked she milked her goat, so that they might have a little milk with them.
sentences.n: derweil = while, in the meantime — an old word the tale uses again later. “damit … hätten” is a purpose clause with the subjunctive: so that they might have. A single goat was the poor household’s whole livestock, the cow of those who could not keep a cow.

sentences.t: Und als der Tisch gedeckt war, setzte sich der liebe Gott nieder und aß mit ihnen, und schmeckte ihm die schlechte Kost gut, denn es waren vergnügte Gesichter dabei.
sentences.l: And when the table was laid, the dear God sat down and ate with them, and the poor fare tasted good to him, for there were contented faces at it.
sentences.i: And when the table was laid, the dear Lord sat down and ate with them, and the poor fare tasted good to him, for there were contented faces around it.
sentences.n: “schmeckte ihm die schlechte Kost gut” puts the verb first because the clause hangs on the preceding und — literally “tasted to him the poor fare good”; schmecken takes the dative of the person. Kost is fare, what there is to eat. schlecht here means poor, meagre, not spoiled.

sentences.t: Nachdem sie gegessen hatten, und Schlafenszeit war, rief die Frau heimlich ihren Mann und sprach „hör, lieber Mann, wir wollen uns heute Nacht eine Streu machen, damit der arme Wanderer sich in unser Bett legen und ausruhen kann:
sentences.l: After they had eaten, and it was bedtime, the wife called her husband secretly and spoke “listen, dear husband, we will make ourselves a bed of straw tonight, so that the poor wanderer can lie down in our bed and rest:
sentences.i: When they had eaten and it was time for sleep, the wife quietly called her husband aside and said: “Listen, dear husband, let us make ourselves a straw bed tonight, so that the poor traveller can lie down in our bed and rest;
sentences.n: “wir wollen” is not a wish but a proposal — let us. Streu is loose straw shaken out on the floor for sleeping on, what a household had instead of a second bed. lieber Mann is “dear husband”; Mann does double duty for man and husband.

sentences.t: er ist den ganzen Tag über gegangen, da wird einer müde.“
sentences.l: he has gone the whole day through, that makes one tired.”
sentences.i: he has been walking the whole day long, and that will tire a man.”
sentences.n: “den ganzen Tag über” = all day long, with über again following its noun. einer is the indefinite “one, a man,” where modern German would say man — “that makes one tired.”

sentences.t: „Von Herzen gern,“ antwortete er, „ich wills ihm anbieten,“
sentences.l: “From the heart gladly,” answered he, “I will offer it to him,”
sentences.i: “With all my heart,” he answered; “I will offer it to him,” —
sentences.n: “von Herzen gern” = right willingly, with all one’s heart — the same phrase his wife used of their giving. wills = will es.

sentences.t: gieng zu dem lieben Gott und bat ihn, wenns ihm recht wäre, möcht er sich in ihr Bett legen und seine Glieder ordentlich ausruhen.
sentences.l: went to the dear God and asked him, if it were agreeable to him, he might lay himself in their bed and rest his limbs properly.
sentences.i: and he went to the dear Lord and asked him, if it suited him, to lie down in their bed and rest his limbs properly.
sentences.n: The subject is dropped again after the quotation — “gieng zu dem lieben Gott” carries straight on from er. wäre and möcht are subjunctives of reported speech: the request is given, not quoted. wenns = wenn es; “wenn es ihm recht wäre” = if it were all right by him. ordentlich here means properly, thoroughly.

sentences.t: Der liebe Gott wollte den beiden Alten ihr Lager nicht nehmen, aber sie ließen nicht ab, bis er es endlich that und sich in ihr Bett legte:
sentences.l: The dear God did not want to take their bed from the two old people, but they did not leave off until he at last did it and laid himself in their bed:
sentences.i: The dear Lord had no wish to take the two old people’s bed from them, but they would not give over until at last he did so and lay down in their bed;
sentences.n: “nicht ablassen” = not to leave off, not to give up urging; ab is separable. that is the 1857 spelling of tat, the past of tun. Lager is a place to lie, a bed in the plainest sense.

sentences.t: sich selbst aber machten sie eine Streu auf die Erde.
sentences.l: but for themselves they made a bed of straw on the ground.
sentences.i: but for themselves they made up straw on the floor.
sentences.n: “sich selbst” stands first for contrast, so the verb comes second and the subject last — “sich selbst aber machten sie.” Erde here is the floor of the room, the bare ground.

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen standen sie vor Tag schon auf und kochten dem Gast ein Frühstück, so gut sie es hatten.
sentences.l: The next morning they were up already before day and cooked the guest a breakfast, as good as they had it.
sentences.i: Next morning they were up before daylight and cooked their guest such a breakfast as they were able.
sentences.n: “am andern Morgen” = on the next morning; ander is “the other, the next.” “so gut sie es hatten” = as well as their means allowed — literally as good as they had it. standen … auf is separable aufstehen.

sentences.t: Als nun die Sonne durchs Fensterlein schien und der liebe Gott aufgestanden war, aß er wieder mit ihnen und wollte dann seines Weges ziehen.
sentences.l: When now the sun shone through the little window and the dear God had got up, he ate again with them and wanted then to go his way.
sentences.i: When the sun shone in at the little window and the dear Lord had risen, he ate with them again and was ready to go his way.
sentences.n: “seines Weges ziehen” is a set phrase with a genitive: to go one’s way, travel on. Fensterlein is another diminutive of the poor house; durchs = durch das. wollte here is on the point of, was minded to, rather than a plain wish.

sentences.t: Als er in der Thüre stand, kehrte er sich um und sprach „weil ihr so mitleidig und fromm seid, so wünscht euch dreierlei, das will ich euch erfüllen.“
sentences.l: As he stood in the door, he turned himself round and spoke “because you are so compassionate and pious, so wish yourselves three things, that will I fulfil for you.”
sentences.i: As he stood in the doorway he turned round and said: “Because you are so compassionate and God-fearing, wish three wishes, and I will fulfil them for you.”
sentences.n: A subordinate clause with weil throws its verb to the end — “weil ihr so mitleidig und fromm seid” — and the main clause then begins with so, resuming it. dreierlei is “three kinds of thing,” an old counting-word; wünscht euch is the plural imperative with the reflexive dative. fromm is pious, godly, and also good in the old wide sense.

sentences.t: Da sagte der Arme „was soll ich mir sonst wünschen als die ewige Seligkeit, und daß wir zwei, so lang wir leben, gesund dabei bleiben und unser nothdürftiges tägliches Brot haben;
sentences.l: Then the poor man said “what should I wish myself other than eternal blessedness, and that we two, as long as we live, stay healthy along with it and have our needful daily bread;
sentences.i: Then the poor man said: “What should I wish for but eternal salvation, and that the two of us stay in health as long as we live and have our daily bread as we need it;
sentences.n: “was soll ich mir sonst wünschen als …” = what should I wish for other than. “die ewige Seligkeit” is eternal blessedness, salvation — the first thing a pious man asks. “unser nothdürftiges tägliches Brot” echoes the Lord’s Prayer, with nothdürftig (1857 spelling of notdürftig) meaning just enough for need, no more. dabei = along with that, into the bargain.

sentences.t: fürs dritte weiß ich mir nichts zu wünschen.“
sentences.l: for the third I know nothing to wish myself.”
sentences.i: as for the third, I know of nothing to wish for.”
sentences.n: fürs = für das; “fürs dritte” = thirdly, as the third. “weiß ich mir nichts zu wünschen” — wissen with zu + infinitive is to know of a thing to do, to be able to think of one.

sentences.t: Der liebe Gott sprach „willst du dir nicht ein neues Haus für das alte wünschen?“
sentences.l: The dear God spoke “will you not wish yourself a new house for the old one?”
sentences.i: The dear Lord said: “Will you not wish for a new house in place of the old one?”
sentences.n: The dative of the person wishing — dir — is what German adds and English drops: wish yourself. Note that God says du to the poor man, though the poor man says ihr to him.

sentences.t: „O ja,“ sagte der Mann, „wenn ich das auch noch erhalten kann, so wär mirs wohl lieb.“
sentences.l: “O yes,” said the man, “if I can get that as well, then it would be right dear to me.”
sentences.i: “Oh yes,” said the man, “if I may have that too, I should like it well enough.”
sentences.n: wär and mirs (= mir es) are the clipped spoken forms the tales print without apology; wär is subjunctive — it would be. “lieb sein” with the dative = to be welcome, pleasing to someone. erhalten here is to receive, get, not to preserve.

sentences.t: Da erfüllte der Herr ihre Wünsche, verwandelte ihr altes Haus in ein neues, gab ihnen nochmals seinen Segen und zog weiter.
sentences.l: Then the Lord fulfilled their wishes, changed their old house into a new one, gave them once more his blessing and went further.
sentences.i: Then the Lord granted their wishes, turned their old house into a new one, gave them his blessing once more and journeyed on.
sentences.n: “verwandeln in” takes the accusative: changed it into a new one. “zog weiter” — weiterziehen, to travel on, separable; ziehen of a traveller is to move on, not to pull.

sentences.t: Es war schon voller Tag, als der Reiche aufstand.
sentences.l: It was already full day when the rich man got up.
sentences.i: It was broad daylight before the rich man rose.
sentences.n: “voller Tag” = full day, broad daylight — the sluggard’s hour, set against the poor couple who were up before dawn. aufstand is separable aufstehen with its prefix at the end of the clause.

sentences.t: Er legte sich ins Fenster und sah gegenüber ein neues, reinliches Haus mit rothen Ziegeln, wo sonst eine alte Hütte gestanden hatte.
sentences.l: He laid himself in the window and saw opposite a new, clean house with red tiles, where otherwise an old hut had stood.
sentences.i: He leaned out at the window and saw across the way a new, trim house with red tiles, where an old hut had stood before.
sentences.n: “sich ins Fenster legen” is to lean out over the sill on one’s elbows, the householder’s posture. sonst here means formerly, at other times, not “otherwise.” roth is the 1857 spelling of rot; red roof-tiles mean a solid house, where the hut would have had thatch.

sentences.t: Da machte er große Augen, rief seine Frau herbei und sprach „sag mir, was ist geschehen?
sentences.l: Then he made big eyes, called his wife over and spoke “tell me, what has happened?
sentences.i: Then he opened his eyes wide, called his wife over and said: “Tell me, what has happened?
sentences.n: “große Augen machen” = to stare, to be astonished — the idiom is still current. herbeirufen is separable: rief … herbei, called her to the spot.

sentences.t: Gestern Abend stand noch die alte elende Hütte, und heute steht da ein schönes neues Haus.
sentences.l: Yesterday evening the old wretched hut was still standing, and today there stands a fine new house.
sentences.i: Last night the old wretched hut was still standing, and today a fine new house stands there.
sentences.n: noch here is “still, as yet.” The time-word stands first in each half, so the verb comes second and the subject follows it — “Gestern Abend stand … und heute steht …” — the ordinary German V2 order.

sentences.t: Lauf hinüber und höre wie das gekommen ist.“
sentences.l: Run over and hear how that has come about.”
sentences.i: Run over and find out how that came about.”
sentences.n: hören is used for getting news, hence “find out.” “wie das gekommen ist” = how that has come to be. Both verbs are the singular imperative — he says du to his wife, as the poor couple do to one another.

sentences.t: Die Frau gieng und fragte den Armen aus:
sentences.l: The wife went and questioned the poor man out:
sentences.i: The wife went across and questioned the poor man:
sentences.n: “jemanden ausfragen” = to question someone thoroughly, to pump him for news; the prefix aus stands at the end. gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging.

sentences.t: er erzählte ihr „gestern Abend kam ein Wanderer, der suchte Nachtherberge, und heute Morgen beim Abschied hat er uns drei Wünsche gewährt, die ewige Seligkeit, Gesundheit in diesem Leben und das nothdürftige tägliche Brot dazu und zuletzt noch statt unserer alten Hütte ein schönes neues Haus.“
sentences.l: he told her “yesterday evening there came a wanderer, he sought night-shelter, and this morning at parting he has granted us three wishes, eternal blessedness, health in this life and the needful daily bread along with it, and last of all, instead of our old hut, a fine new house.”
sentences.i: and he told her: “Last night a traveller came who was looking for a night’s shelter, and this morning at parting he granted us three wishes: eternal salvation, health in this life and our daily bread as we need it, and last of all a fine new house in place of our old hut.”
sentences.n: der here is a demonstrative doing the work of a relative — “ein Wanderer, der suchte” — literally “a wanderer, he sought.” “beim Abschied” = at the leave-taking. statt takes the genitive: statt unserer alten Hütte. Note how the poor man’s report quietly promotes the modest wishes into a list of gifts.

sentences.t: Die Frau des Reichen lief eilig zurück und erzählte ihrem Manne wie alles gekommen war.
sentences.l: The wife of the rich man ran hastily back and told her husband how everything had come about.
sentences.i: The rich man’s wife ran hurriedly back and told her husband how it had all come about.
sentences.n: Manne keeps the old dative -e, still usual in 1857 where we now write Mann. eilig = hastily, in a hurry.

sentences.t: Der Mann sprach „ich möchte mich zerreißen und zerschlagen:
sentences.l: The man spoke “I could tear myself apart and beat myself to pieces:
sentences.i: The man said: “I could tear myself to pieces and thrash myself:
sentences.n: “ich möchte mich zerreißen und zerschlagen” is a violent idiom of self-reproach — I could tear my hair, I could kick myself. möchte is the subjunctive of mögen: I could, I would like to.

sentences.t: hätt ich das nur gewußt!
sentences.l: had I only known that!
sentences.i: if only I had known!
sentences.n: A wish with no wenn: the verb stands first — “hätt ich das nur gewußt” — and the subjunctive hätt carries the regret. nur in such a wish is “only, if only.”

sentences.t: der Fremde ist zuvor hier gewesen und hat bei uns übernachten wollen, ich habe ihn aber abgewiesen.“
sentences.l: the stranger has been here before and wanted to stay the night with us, but I turned him away.”
sentences.i: the stranger was here first and wanted to lodge with us, and I turned him away.”
sentences.n: zuvor = beforehand, first. “hat … übernachten wollen” is the double infinitive that replaces the participle after a modal — literally “has wanted to stay the night.” abweisen = to turn away, refuse, separable.

sentences.t: „Eil dich,“ sprach die Frau, „und setze dich auf dein Pferd, so kannst du den Mann noch einholen, und dann mußt du dir auch drei Wünsche gewähren lassen.“
sentences.l: “Hurry yourself,” spoke the wife, “and set yourself on your horse, then you can still catch the man up, and then you must have three wishes granted you too.”
sentences.i: “Make haste,” said the wife, “and get on your horse; you can still overtake the man, and then you must have three wishes granted you as well.”
sentences.n: sich eilen is reflexive: hurry yourself. einholen = to catch up with, overtake, separable. “sich … gewähren lassen” — lassen + infinitive again, to have a thing granted to oneself; German puts the person in the dative, dir.

sentences.t: Der Reiche befolgte den guten Rath, jagte mit seinem Pferd davon und holte den lieben Gott noch ein.
sentences.l: The rich man followed the good advice, galloped off with his horse and caught the dear God up after all.
sentences.i: The rich man took the good advice, galloped off on his horse and did overtake the dear Lord.
sentences.n: Rath is the 1857 spelling of Rat, advice — not the same word as the council-Rat, though spelled alike. befolgen takes a plain accusative: to follow, obey advice. “holte … ein” is separable einholen, and noch here means “still, after all, in time.”

sentences.t: Er redete fein und lieblich und bat er möchts nicht übel nehmen, daß er nicht gleich wäre eingelassen worden, er hätte den Schlüssel zur Hausthüre gesucht, derweil wäre er weggegangen:
sentences.l: He talked fine and sweetly and asked he might not take it ill that he had not been let in at once, he had been looking for the key to the house-door, meanwhile he had gone away:
sentences.i: He spoke smoothly and pleasantly and begged him not to take it amiss that he had not been let in at once: he had been looking for the key to the house door, and in the meantime the stranger had gone away;
sentences.n: Everything after bat is subjunctive of reported speech — möchts, wäre eingelassen worden, hätte gesucht, wäre weggegangen — which is how the tale can hand on his excuse without endorsing a word of it. “übel nehmen” = to take amiss, take ill; möchts = möchte es. derweil = in the meantime, as earlier in the tale.

sentences.t: wenn er des Weges zurück käme, müßte er bei ihm einkehren.
sentences.l: if he should come back this way, he must put up with him.
sentences.i: if he came back this way, he must be sure to lodge with him.
sentences.n: “des Weges” is a genitive of the road travelled: this way, along the road. einkehren = to turn in, put up at a house for the night. käme and müßte keep the reported speech running, and müßte here is pressing invitation rather than compulsion.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ sprach der liebe Gott, „wenn ich einmal zurückkomme, will ich es thun.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” spoke the dear God, “if I ever come back, I will do it.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” said the dear Lord, “if I come back this way one day, I will do so.”
sentences.n: einmal here is “one day, at some time,” not “once.” thun is the 1857 spelling of tun.

sentences.t: Da fragte der Reiche ob er nicht auch drei Wünsche thun dürfte, wie sein Nachbar?
sentences.l: Then the rich man asked whether he might not do three wishes too, like his neighbour?
sentences.i: Then the rich man asked whether he too might not make three wishes, like his neighbour.
sentences.n: The question mark stands although the question is reported, not quoted — the same habit as at the rich man’s window earlier. dürfte is subjunctive: whether he might. “Wünsche thun” is the old idiom, to do wishes where we say make them.

sentences.t: Ja, sagte der liebe Gott, das dürfte er wohl, es wäre aber nicht gut für ihn, und er sollte sich lieber nichts wünschen.
sentences.l: Yes, said the dear God, he might well do so, but it would not be good for him, and he had better wish himself nothing.
sentences.i: Yes, said the dear Lord, he might well; but it would do him no good, and he would do better to wish for nothing.
sentences.n: The whole answer is reported speech in the subjunctive — dürfte, wäre, sollte — and the opening Ja stands unquoted inside it, so that the warning comes at one remove. “lieber nichts” = better nothing, rather nothing.

sentences.t: Der Reiche meinte er wollte sich schon etwas aussuchen, das zu seinem Glück gereiche, wenn er nur wüßte, daß es erfüllt würde.
sentences.l: The rich man thought he would surely pick something out for himself that turned to his good fortune, if only he knew that it would be fulfilled.
sentences.i: The rich man reckoned he would find something to choose that would turn to his own good fortune, if only he could be sure it would be granted.
sentences.n: meinen here is to be of the opinion, to reckon, not to mean. “sich etwas aussuchen” = to pick something out for oneself, separable aus-. gereichen with zu is a stiff older verb: to redound to, turn to. schon is the confident little word — surely, no fear of that.

sentences.t: Sprach der liebe Gott „reit heim, und drei Wünsche, die du thust, die sollen in Erfüllung gehen.“
sentences.l: Spoke the dear God “ride home, and three wishes that you do, those shall go into fulfilment.”
sentences.i: The dear Lord said: “Ride home; and three wishes that you make shall be fulfilled.”
sentences.n: The sentence begins with its verb — “Sprach der liebe Gott” — the same lively inversion the tale used when it dropped the subject altogether at “Schlug damit sein Fenster zu.” “in Erfüllung gehen” = to come true, be fulfilled. die … die takes up the wishes twice, once as relative and once as demonstrative, which German allows and English does not.

sentences.t: Nun hatte der Reiche was er verlangte, ritt heimwärts und fieng an nachzusinnen was er sich wünschen sollte.
sentences.l: Now the rich man had what he demanded, rode homewards and began to ponder what he should wish himself.
sentences.i: Now the rich man had what he had asked for; he rode homewards and began to ponder what he should wish for.
sentences.n: fieng is the 1857 spelling of fing, the past of anfangen, which is separable — “fieng an … nachzusinnen,” with zu tucked between prefix and stem in nachzusinnen. verlangen = to demand, ask for. The reflexive dative sich, wishing for oneself, runs through the whole tale.

sentences.t: Wie er sich so bedachte und die Zügel fallen ließ, fieng das Pferd an zu springen, so daß er immerfort in seinen Gedanken gestört wurde und sie gar nicht zusammen bringen konnte.
sentences.l: As he thought to himself so and let the reins fall, the horse began to spring, so that he was continually disturbed in his thoughts and could not bring them together at all.
sentences.i: While he was pondering in this way and let the reins fall slack, the horse began to prance, so that he was for ever being disturbed in his thoughts and could not collect them at all.
sentences.n: Wie at the head of a clause means “as, while,” not “how.” “sich bedenken” = to think a matter over. “die Gedanken zusammen bringen” = to collect one’s thoughts. sie takes up Gedanken; “gar nicht” = not at all.

sentences.t: Er klopfte ihm an den Hals und sagte „sei ruhig, Liese,“ aber das Pferd machte aufs neue Männerchen.
sentences.l: He knocked it on the neck and said “be quiet, Liese,” but the horse made its little-man afresh.
sentences.i: He patted it on the neck and said, “Steady, Liese,” but the horse reared up again.
sentences.n: German puts the creature in the dative and the part struck in the accusative — “klopfte ihm an den Hals” — where English says “patted it on the neck.” “Männerchen machen” is said of a horse rearing up on its hind legs, as a little man might stand. Liese is a common name for a mare. “aufs neue” = afresh, once again.

sentences.t: Da ward er zuletzt ärgerlich und rief ganz ungeduldig „so wollt ich, daß du den Hals zerbrächst!“
sentences.l: Then he grew angry at last and cried quite impatiently “so I wish that you might break your neck!”
sentences.i: At last he lost his temper and cried out impatiently: “I wish you would break your neck!”
sentences.n: ward is the old past of werden, modern wurde: he became angry. zerbrächst is the past subjunctive of zerbrechen, which is what makes this a wish and not a statement — and a wish is exactly the wrong thing for him to be uttering. “den Hals brechen” = to break one’s neck.

sentences.t: Wie er das Wort ausgesprochen hatte, plump, fiel er auf die Erde, und lag das Pferd todt und regte sich nicht mehr;
sentences.l: When he had spoken the word out, plump, he fell on the earth, and the horse lay dead and stirred no more;
sentences.i: The moment the word was out of his mouth — plump — he fell to the ground, and there lay the horse dead and stirred no more;
sentences.n: plump is the sound of the fall standing alone where a verb would be. The subject is dropped in “und lag das Pferd todt,” which begins with its verb. todt is the 1857 spelling of tot; “sich regen” = to stir, move.

sentences.t: damit war der erste Wunsch erfüllt.
sentences.l: with that the first wish was fulfilled.
sentences.n: damit = with that, therewith — the tale’s dry way of counting off the wishes as they are spent.

sentences.t: Weil er aber von Natur geizig war, wollte er das Sattelzeug nicht im Stich lassen, schnitts ab, hiengs auf seinen Rücken, und mußte nun zu Fuß gehen.
sentences.l: But because he was by nature miserly, he did not want to leave the saddle-gear in the lurch, cut it off, hung it on his back, and now had to go on foot.
sentences.i: But because he was miserly by nature, he would not abandon the saddle and harness: he cut them off, hung them on his back, and now had to go on foot.
sentences.n: “im Stich lassen” = to leave in the lurch, abandon — said here of a thing rather than a person, which is part of the joke. schnitts = schnitt es, hiengs = hieng es (hieng being the 1857 spelling of hing). Sattelzeug is the whole harness, saddle and gear together.

sentences.t: „Du hast noch zwei Wünsche übrig“ dachte er und tröstete sich damit.
sentences.l: “You have two wishes left over” he thought and comforted himself with that.
sentences.n: He addresses himself as du — talking to oneself in the second person is ordinary in these tales. “übrig haben” = to have remaining, left over. Note that the thought is punctuated as speech but takes no comma before dachte.

sentences.t: Wie er nun langsam durch den Sand dahin gieng, und zu Mittag die Sonne heiß brannte, wards ihm so warm und verdrießlich zu Muth:
sentences.l: When he now went slowly along through the sand, and at midday the sun burned hot, it grew so warm and peevish to him in his mind:
sentences.i: Now as he trudged slowly on through the sand, and at noon the sun burned hot, he began to feel hot and ill-tempered;
sentences.n: “zu Muth werden” is a fixed impersonal expression for how one feels within: “wards ihm warm zu Muth” = his mind grew hot, he felt hot and vexed. wards = ward es. verdrießlich = peevish, out of humour. dahin gieng — dahingehen, to walk along, on and on.

sentences.t: der Sattel drückte ihn auf den Rücken, auch war ihm noch immer nicht eingefallen, was er sich wünschen sollte.
sentences.l: the saddle pressed him on the back, and it still had not occurred to him what he should wish himself.
sentences.i: the saddle pressed on his back, and still it had not come into his head what he ought to wish for.
sentences.n: “einfallen” with the dative is the German for a thought striking one — literally it falls in to him; the prefix ein stands at the end. auch here is little more than “moreover, besides.”

sentences.t: „Wenn ich mir auch alle Reiche und Schätze der Welt wünsche,“ sprach er zu sich selbst, „so fällt mir hernach noch allerlei ein, dieses und jenes, das weiß ich im voraus:
sentences.l: “Even if I wish myself all the kingdoms and treasures of the world,” he spoke to himself, “then afterwards all sorts of things will still occur to me, this and that, I know that in advance:
sentences.i: “Even if I wish for all the kingdoms and treasures of the world,” he said to himself, “I shall think of all manner of things afterwards, this and that — I know it beforehand;
sentences.n: Reiche here is the plural of das Reich, realm, kingdom — not the rich men of the title, though the two words look alike. “fällt mir … ein” is einfallen again, now with allerlei as its subject: all sorts of things will come into my head. “im voraus” = beforehand, in advance.

sentences.t: ich wills aber so einrichten, daß mir gar nichts mehr übrig zu wünschen bleibt.“
sentences.l: but I will arrange it so that nothing at all remains over for me to wish.”
sentences.i: but I will so arrange it that nothing at all is left for me to wish for.”
sentences.n: wills = will es; einrichten = to arrange, set up, separable. “übrig zu wünschen bleibt” — zu + infinitive with bleiben: remains to be wished. He is trying to make a wish that closes off all further wishing, which is where such tales always trip a man up.

sentences.t: Dann seufzte er und sprach „ja, wenn ich der bairische Bauer wäre, der auch drei Wünsche frei hatte, der wußte sich zu helfen,
sentences.l: Then he sighed and spoke “yes, if I were the Bavarian peasant, who also had three wishes free, he knew how to help himself,
sentences.i: Then he sighed and said: “Ah, if only I were the Bavarian peasant who also had three wishes granted him — he knew how to help himself:
sentences.n: wäre is the past subjunctive of the contrary-to-fact wish: if I were. der at the head of the next clauses is a demonstrative, “that one, he,” not a relative — the tale keeps pointing back at the peasant with it. “sich zu helfen wissen” = to know how to shift for oneself. The Bavarian peasant is a stock figure from another wish-tale, told as though the listeners knew him.

sentences.t: der wünschte sich zuerst recht viel Bier, und zweitens so viel Bier als er trinken könnte, und drittens noch ein Faß Bier dazu.“
sentences.l: he wished himself first a right lot of beer, and secondly as much beer as he could drink, and thirdly a cask of beer besides.”
sentences.i: first he wished for a great deal of beer, and secondly for as much beer as he could drink, and thirdly for a cask of beer besides.”
sentences.n: recht viel = a right lot, a good deal. The joke is that the peasant’s third wish adds nothing to the second — and the rich man, who thinks himself cleverer, will do worse. könnte is subjunctive: as much as he might be able to drink.

sentences.t: Manchmal meinte er jetzt hätte er es gefunden, aber hernach schiens ihm doch zu wenig.
sentences.l: Sometimes he thought he had now found it, but afterwards it seemed to him too little after all.
sentences.i: Now and then he thought he had hit on it, but afterwards it seemed too little to him after all.
sentences.n: hätte and schiens (= schien es) mark the report of his thinking: he thought he had found it. hernach = afterwards, thereafter. doch again concedes what he cannot get round.

sentences.t: Da kam ihm so in die Gedanken was es seine Frau jetzt gut hätte, die säße daheim in einer kühlen Stube und ließe sichs wohl schmecken.
sentences.l: Then it came to him so into his thoughts how good his wife had it now, she would be sitting at home in a cool room and letting herself be well pleased.
sentences.i: Then it came into his thoughts how well off his wife was just now, sitting at home in a cool room and enjoying herself.
sentences.n: säße and ließe are subjunctives of reported thought — this is what he imagines, not what the tale asserts. “es gut haben” = to have it good, be well off. “sichs wohl schmecken lassen” is a fixed phrase for enjoying one’s food and comfort; sichs = sich es.

sentences.t: Das ärgerte ihn ordentlich, und ohne daß ers wußte, sprach er so hin „ich wollte die säße daheim auf dem Sattel, und könnte nicht herunter, statt daß ich ihn da auf meinem Rücken schleppe.“
sentences.l: That vexed him properly, and without his knowing it, he spoke so away “I wish she were sitting at home on the saddle, and could not get down, instead of my dragging it here on my back.”
sentences.i: That vexed him thoroughly, and without knowing what he was doing he said out loud: “I wish she were sitting at home on the saddle and could not get down, instead of my hauling it about on my back.”
sentences.n: “so hin sprechen” is to say a thing carelessly, into the air — which is exactly how the second wish is spent. ers = er es. “ich wollte die säße” has no daß: the wish clause simply follows, with die as a demonstrative for his wife and the subjunctive säße carrying the wishing. “statt daß” = instead of the fact that.

sentences.t: Und wie das letzte Wort aus seinem Munde kam, so war der Sattel von seinem Rücken verschwunden, und er merkte daß sein zweiter Wunsch auch in Erfüllung gegangen war.
sentences.l: And as the last word came out of his mouth, so the saddle was vanished from his back, and he noticed that his second wish too had gone into fulfilment.
sentences.i: And as the last word left his mouth, the saddle was gone from his back, and he saw that his second wish too had been fulfilled.
sentences.n: German forms the perfect of verschwinden with sein — “war … verschwunden,” was vanished — as it does with all verbs of change of place or state. The so answering wie is the resuming “then” of older narrative.

sentences.t: Da ward ihm erst recht heiß, er fieng an zu laufen und wollte sich daheim ganz einsam in seine Kammer hinsetzen und auf etwas Großes für den letzten Wunsch sinnen.
sentences.l: Then it grew hot to him only the more, he began to run and wanted to sit himself down at home quite alone in his chamber and think on something great for the last wish.
sentences.i: Now he grew hotter than ever; he began to run, meaning to sit down at home quite alone in his room and think out something great for the last wish.
sentences.n: “erst recht” = all the more, more than ever — the phrase turns a setback into an increase. “auf etwas sinnen” = to meditate on, plot at something. hinsetzen is separable, and the whole string of infinitives waits for the modal wollte at the front.

sentences.t: Wie er aber ankommt und die Stubenthür aufmacht, sitzt da seine Frau mittendrin auf dem Sattel und kann nicht herunter, jammert und schreit.
sentences.l: But when he arrives and opens the parlour door, there sits his wife in the middle of it on the saddle and cannot get down, wails and screams.
sentences.i: But when he arrives and opens the parlour door, there sits his wife in the middle of the room on the saddle, unable to get down, wailing and screaming.
sentences.n: The tale jumps into the present tense — ankommt, aufmacht, sitzt — for the moment of discovery, as a teller does at the point of the joke. Stubenthür is the door of the Stube, the one heated living room of the house; the 1857 spelling keeps th. mittendrin = right in the middle of it.

sentences.t: Da sprach er „gib dich zufrieden, ich will dir alle Reichthümer der Welt herbei wünschen, nur bleib da sitzen.“
sentences.l: Then he spoke “content yourself, I will wish you all the riches of the world here, only stay sitting there.”
sentences.i: Then he said: “Be content — I will wish all the riches of the world here for you; only stay sitting where you are.”
sentences.n: “gib dich zufrieden” = be satisfied, calm yourself, an old imperative phrase. “herbei wünschen” is to wish a thing here, to summon it by wishing; herbei is the same prefix he used of calling his wife over at the window.

sentences.t: Sie schalt ihn aber einen Schafskopf und sprach „was helfen mir alle Reichthümer der Welt, wenn ich auf dem Sattel sitze;
sentences.l: But she scolded him a sheep’s-head and spoke “what help to me are all the riches of the world, if I am sitting on the saddle;
sentences.i: But she called him a blockhead and said: “What good are all the riches of the world to me while I am sitting on the saddle?
sentences.n: schelten takes two accusatives — to scold someone something, to call him a name to his face. Schafskopf, sheep’s-head, is a blockhead, a fool. “was helfen mir …” = what use are they to me, with the person in the dative.

sentences.t: du hast mich darauf gewünscht, du mußt mir auch wieder herunter helfen.“
sentences.l: you have wished me onto it, you must help me down again too.”
sentences.i: you wished me onto it, and you must help me down off it again.”
sentences.n: darauf = onto it, referring to the saddle. The second half has no und: two clauses set side by side, the second the plain consequence of the first, which is how German scolding runs.

sentences.t: Er mochte wollen oder nicht, er mußte den dritten Wunsch thun, daß sie vom Sattel ledig wäre und herunter steigen könnte; und der Wunsch ward alsbald erfüllt.
sentences.l: He might want to or not, he had to do the third wish, that she should be free of the saddle and could climb down; and the wish was fulfilled forthwith.
sentences.i: Whether he liked it or not, he had to make the third wish, that she might be rid of the saddle and could climb down; and the wish was granted at once.
sentences.n: “Er mochte wollen oder nicht” = whether he would or not, willy-nilly. ledig here is free of, rid of — its old sense, before it came to mean unmarried. ward is again the old past of werden, forming the passive; alsbald = forthwith, straightway.

sentences.t: Also hatte er nichts davon als Ärger, Mühe, Scheltworte und ein verlornes Pferd: die Armen aber lebten vergnügt, still und fromm bis an ihr seliges Ende.
sentences.l: So he had nothing from it but vexation, trouble, scolding-words and a lost horse: but the poor people lived contented, quiet and pious until their blessed end.
sentences.i: So he had nothing out of it but vexation, trouble, hard words and a horse the less; but the poor couple lived contented, quiet and godly to their blessed end.
sentences.n: Also here is “thus, so,” closing the tale as it opened the rich man’s rebuff. “nichts davon haben als …” = to have nothing out of it but. verlornes is the older form of verlorenes. “ihr seliges Ende” is a blessed end, a good Christian death — the very thing the poor man wished for first, and the rich man never thought of.

glossary.aufstand: aufstehen — got up, rose (3 sg. past; separable auf-)
glossary.eil: sich eilen — hurry! (imperative sg., eil dich: make haste)
glossary.liese: Liese — Liese, here the mare’s name (a common name for a horse; not leise, softly)
glossary.ließen: ablassen — left off, gave over (3 pl. past, sie ließen nicht ab: they would not give over)
glossary.männerchen: das Männchen — little man; “Männerchen machen” is said of a horse rearing on its hind legs
glossary.reiche: reich; das Reich — (der Reiche) the rich man; (alle Reiche) the realms, kingdoms
glossary.setze: setzen — set, seat (imperative sg., setze dich auf dein Pferd: get on your horse)
glossary.stich: der Stich — prick, stab; in “im Stich lassen” = to leave in the lurch, abandon
glossary.streu: die Streu — loose straw shaken out to sleep on (eine Streu machen: to make up a straw bed)
glossary.suche: suchen — is seeking (3 sg. present subjunctive of reported speech: was er suche)
glossary.wandelte: wandeln — walked, went about (3 sg. past; auf Erden wandeln, to walk the earth)
glossary.weiß: wissen — (I) know (1 sg. present; not the adjective weiß, white)
